title: deal-synthesis-brief-economics-and-program-design-2026
author: Maya Patel
content:
Overview:
This brief equips field sellers and solution engineers with a compact, repeatable program for synthesizing technical economics and commercial design when engaging mid‑market and enterprise buyers. It combines crisp persona messaging, pricing scenarios, architectural deal patterns, and an embedded security FAQ that can be shared with prospects under NDA.

Intended audience:
- Sales engineers and account executives (technical and commercial)
- Deal desk and solution architects
- Customer success for pilot-to-production transition

One‑line pitch for each buyer persona:
- CTO / Head of Platform: "Predictable inference costs and consistent latency across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments — control economics without building your own stack."
- Platform Engineer / MLE: "Drop-in API, model version pinning, and automated batching/caching that reduces token cost by up to 3x in typical workloads."
- Security / InfoSec: "Private deployment and KMS/HSM integrations with audit logs and RBAC for production compliance."

Key messages (3 pillars):
1) Production economics: measurable per-token and per-request savings via batching, prefix caching, and quantization profiles. Include conservative, typical, and aggressive uplift estimates for pilots.
2) Deployment parity: same API surface and observability regardless of Hosted, Dedicated, or Private modes — reduces integration risk and accelerates rollout.
3) Risk mitigation: fallbacks and routing policies to maintain availability, plus compliance features required by regulated buyers.

Competitive brief (short):
- Major cloud AI endpoints (C1): strong ecosystem, weak cost transparency and custom kernel optimizations. Redwood advantage: predictable unit economics, kernel selection for long contexts, and cost-aware routing.
- LLM API pure-plays (C2): broad model catalog but limited deployment parity for private/offline use. Redwood advantage: unified runtime across private and hosted with enterprise features.
- Self-hosted inference stacks (C3): full control, high engineering lift, slower iteration. Redwood advantage: offloads operational burden while preserving deployment control via Private offering.

Pricing guidance framework (pilot → production):
- Pilot (Proof-of-concept, 4–8 weeks): discounted hosted credits or temporary Dedicated slice. Typical ask: 20K–50K credits.
- Ramp (3–6 months): committed monthly baseline for Dedicated with burst allowance; price banding tied to token volumes and model family.
- Production (12–36 month): Reserved capacity with annual commit + negotiated support / SLA annex.

Pricing bands (example for conversation/assistant workloads):
| Stage | Throughput target | Indicative monthly commit | Notes |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Pilot | 50–200 reqs/hr | $10K–$25K | Short-lived, fast ramp |
| Ramp | 1K–10K reqs/hr | $25K–$150K | Needs autoscale & quantization tuning |
| Production | 10K+ reqs/hr | $150K+ | Dedicated pools, private option |

Deal architecture patterns (pick one):
1) Hosted-first pilot → Dedicated convert: fastest time-to-first-result; convert to Dedicated by increasing committed slice and adding SLA. Steps:
   1. Sign pilot terms and NDAs (1 week)
   2. Enable hosted trial with sample models + telemetry dashboards (1–2 days)
   3. Run canonical workload with Redwood Optimize recommendations (2–4 weeks)
   4. Propose Dedicated commit with burst policy and optional Private evaluation (decision meeting)

2) Private evaluation (sec‑sensitive):
   1. Kickoff scoping call (networking, KMS, data flow)
   2. Provide on‑prem packaging checklist and preliminary BOM
   3. Short integration sprint (2–4 weeks) with telemetry and trace hooks
   4. Pilot acceptance tests and sign off

3) Hybrid (Active/Passive split): keep low-latency traffic on Dedicated, failover and heavy-batch jobs to Hosted to optimize cost.

Value calculators and artifacts to bring to the meeting:
- Token consumption model (CSV example) — show current cost, projected cost after batching/quantization, and payback period for Dedicated commit.
- Latency SLO worksheet (p50/p95/p99 targets) and fallback plan.
- Short readiness checklist for Private: network, storage, KMS, audit endpoint.

Sales battlecards: top objections and suggested responses:
- Objection: "We can build this ourselves." Response: "You can, but typical infra TTM is 6–18 months and carries unknown ops cost. Redwood reduces this to weeks with measurable savings and enterprise controls."
- Objection: "We control data if on-prem only." Response: "We offer Private deployments with customer-managed KMS and detailed audit logs; we also support VPC peering and air-gapped packaging."
- Objection: "Price looks high compared to raw GPU hours." Response: "Raw GPU cost is only one part — we optimize kernel selection, batching, and model variants to reduce per-token cost and hidden engineering overhead."

Case study snapshot (compact):
- Customer: Acme Finance (mid-market fintech)
- Challenge: interactive assistant with strict latency (p95 < 400ms) and data residency needs
- Approach: Hosted pilot → Dedicated commit with 2:1 caching + quantization profile; Private demo for audit team
- Outcome: 45% reduction in per-interaction cost, p95 latency 350ms, successful SOC2 readiness evidence provided

Embedded security FAQ (short):
Q: What deployment modes support customer key control?
A: Dedicated supports integration with customer KMS for key rotation. Private (on‑prem/VPC) gives full customer key control and HSM options.
Q: Do we provide audit logs for evaluator requests?
A: Yes — request/response hashes, model version, route and user principal, configurable retention.
Q: How is data at rest encrypted?
A: Default AES-256; for Private we support customer-provided keys and HSM-backed wrapping.
Q: Can you do a vulnerability scan/pen test?
A: Yes — we provide scoping documents and will coordinate with our security team under NDA.

Go‑to cadence for running a successful pilot (playbook):
1) Week 0: Align on success criteria (latency target, unit cost target, compliance checklist)
2) Week 1: Provision trial, ingest sample prompts, baseline metrics
3) Weeks 2–4: Apply Redwood Optimize recommendations, iterate on prompts and quantization, collect evals
4) Week 5: Final review and recommendation (convert, extend, or stop)

Appendix — ownership and escalation:
- Field owner: Solutions Engineering (SE Lead: Jordan Kim)
- Commercial owner: AE (named in opportunity)
- Legal: standard pilot MSA + security annex
- Escalation path: SE -> SE Manager -> Product Security -> VP Sales

Related pages and artifacts to attach to an opportunity:
- Token-cost-calculator-template (attach CSV)
- Security on-boarding checklist (conformance matrix)
- Pilot acceptance test plan (templated tests)
